subtopic: CHINESE SITUATION
CHINESE SITUATION
speechtext:
1.	What has Canada done to protect Canadians in China during the present disturbances in that country?
2.	What protection is now being afforded such Canadians and at whose expense?
3.	If Canada is contributing to the expense of such protection, how and to whom is the contribution made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CHINESE SITUATION
speechtext:
This question relates to the situation in China and I will therefore read to the House the reply which I propose to make to it. The
reply will perhaps serve to answer other questions on the order paper and what it might otherwise be necessary to say in reference to one of the motions of which notice has been given.
The protection of life and property, in any country, whether of nationals or of aliens, is primarily the duty of the government of that country. Of latte, civil war in China, now of several years' duration, has increased the difficulty of ensuring that protection, and the evacuation of certain interior areas by foreign residents has been considered an advisable precaution. At the same time it must be recognized that the loss of life by foreigners in these yearn of disturbance has been extraordinarily small. So far >as is known, only one Canadian has been killed; the existence of a political motive in that case, which occurred in June, 1926, was not fully established, and 'the murderer was shot immediately by Chinese soldiers.
Canada is in full sympathy with the desire, of the Chinese people to secure control of their own destiny, having due regard to the safety of the life and property of foreign residents. While there are extremist elements in the situation, it is clear that as regards the responsible leaders and 'the great majority of the Chinese people, the present nationalist movement is directed, noit against the lives or private rights of foreign residents but against the special! privileges or the measure of control over Chinese affairs exercised by foreign countries as regards extra-territoriality, customs, concessions and other matters. Canada has not in the past had any part in shaping or maintaining the policy of acquiring such rights or privileges in China, and has had no part in the recent hegotiations for their readjustment. The Canadian government is, however, in full sympathy with the British Foreign Secretary's announced policy of "going as far as possible to meet the legitimate aspirations of the Chinese nation," and believes that this course is both just and best adapted to ensure protection of life and of religious and business interests.
Under these circumstances it is not considered that it would serve any useful purpose to propose despatching Canadian forces to China. If the situation should change the government will take the earliest opportunity of consulting with parliament as to the appropriate course to pursue.

speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: SUBSTITUTION OP CANADIAN NATIONAL FOR GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC SECURITIES
speechtext:
The object of the scheme, which can be much better examined in detail when we reach the committee stage on the resolution, is to clear up a difficulty of very long standing in connection with the four per cent perpetual debenture stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, conditionally guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada. As I think every member of the House is aware, there has been difficulty for a number of years with regard to this matter. I think every member of the House knows that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is still to-day in receivership very largely, if not altogether, on account of the difficulty created by this particular issue of stock being outstanding. The issue which we seek to deal with is a perpetual issue; that is to say, it never matures. Anything which is done in connection with it, therefore, must be done either by way of purchase in the open market of the whole stock, which might prove to be difficult, if not impossible, or secondly, by way of negotiation.
I do not propose to go into the history of the difficulty at length, except to say this: as a consequence of the difficulty there undoubtedly has existed in England, and in Europe generally, a feeling that Canada was not dealing fairly with these debenture holders. The matter has been discussed in parliament, and I feel sure that every hon. member present who is familiar with the facts believes that Canada has dealt justly with the holders of the Grand Trunk Pacific perpetual debentures in the past. Just as it takes two parties

Grand Trunk Pacific Ry. Co.
to make a quarrel, however, so also it requires agreement between two parties in order to bring that quarrel to an end-at least where perpetual debentures are concerned-and for some time past negotiations have been conducted with committees representing debenture holders in London with a view to amicable settlement and avoiding litigation. I think I am correct in saying that the arrangement proposed in the bill was reached as between the committee of the debenture holders and representatives of the Canadian National Railway during the month of August, and the arrangement here proposed was, I believe, authorized by the government then in office in the Dominion of Canada. The present government has examined it very carefully in detail, and has no hesitation in recommending it to the consideration of the House. Briefly, it provides that such of the present debentures as are in the hands of the public, amounting to something over seven million pounds, shall be taken up by a new issue of Canadian National debentures, the new issue to bear interest at the rate of two per cent per annum. There is a further provision that two per cent shall be placed in a sinking fund, the proceeds of the sinking fund to be used for the gradual retirement of the debentures.
We can go much more readily into the further details in the committee stage, but in the meantime I should like to say that there is no doubt that there is advantage to Canada and advantage to the Canadian National railways from these points of view. First we have the elimination of the accounting necessary to keep the results of the operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Grand Trank Railway of Canada separate, and make it possible to reduce considerably our accounting work and expense. Another important advantage is that it will enable the present receiver of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to be discharged and permit that company and its lines to be amalgamated with the Canadian National system. I think we may say that another advantage is that this bill, if passed, will eliminate any possibility of a lawsuit which might involve prolonged and expensive litigation, and there is no doubt it will create a better feeling in London and the continent towards Canadian securities and enterprises generally.

speechtext:
This resolution is one of very great importance, and the minister has not given the House all the information about the particular arrangement made with the shareholders in this connection.
The arrangement is not fair to Ontario. About $122,000,000 credit and $22,000,000 cash were taken out of Ontario by the Grand Trunk and invested in the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk, who were the parent company, brought the government in as a quasi partner and when the Grand Trunk Pacific went to the wall a receiver was appointed. A survey was made by the government and the case heard of the holders of the common four per cent stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific company by a royal commission. The Grand Trunk Railway took all this cash and credit out of the old Grand Trunk Railway in Ontario, when the Liberal government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier sanctioned the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific through the parent company, the Grand Trunk Railway. On whose credit? Very largely the Grand Trunk Pacific on the credit of the Grand Trunk railway in the old province of Ontario and the federal government. Ontario suffered untold ills as a result of the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific. We have invested over $2,000,000,000 in the publicly owned roads; about half of this is a frozen asset, pays no interest at all and has no sinking fund. subtopic: REQUEST FOR CORRESPONDENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a question that I should like to ask the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), but in his absence perhaps the right hon. Prime Minister will give me his ear for a moment. For many years there has been pending the question of the status of the Indian tribes of British Columbia and their right or title to lands in that province. To my personal knowledge it has been before the public for seventeen years-I was asked to preside at the first meeting when I was acting mayor of Vancouver some seventeen years ago -and it has been pending ever since, without very much warrant in some respects, and at great expense to the Indians. While I have not much sympathy with some of the views entertained by those who are agitating the question, nevertheless I do think it is desirable to satisfy and quiet the Indians in regard to it. I am anxious to co-operate in giving them every opportunity to have the question settled, but I do not think any headway will be made if it is allowed to drift any longer. I do not say this by way of criticism at all, I offer it rather as a suggestion. I would ask the Prime Minister if the government would consider the appointment of a small select committee to hear the representatives of the Indians and give the question study in order to see if we cannot bring it to a conclusion.

The situation with respect to the fines imposed in connection with the combine in the distribution of fruit and vegetables in western Canada is as follows. The trial in this case resulted in the conviction of four individuals and four companies. The individuals were sentenced to one day each in jail and to a fine of $25,000 each. The corporations were sentenced to fines of $25,000 each. All of the fines imposed, totalling $200,000, were paid immediately following the trial, and no part of them has since been remitted. The amounts were paid into the British Columbia court and subsequently transferred to the provincial treasury. The federal Department of Justice is negotiating with the provincial attorney general with a view to the transfer of these funds to the Receiver General of the Dominion. The cost of the investigation and the prosecution amounted to $116,724.53, the fines therefore exceeding the cost by $83,275.47. the people of Vancouver find out that they were going to get the hotel?
Through the usual channel, the press.

If it will please my hon.
friends opposite, I am quite prepared to believe their statement that they made absolutely no political capital out of the fact that during the election campaign the government of which my hon. friend was a supporter authorized the expenditure of $5,000,000 on a hotel in Vancouver. I am prepared to accept that statement.
Be a man and withdraw the statement. Be a gentleman.
Mr. Chairman, I will-
I should like to believe that my hon. friend is a gentleman and that he will withdraw and apologize for his statement.
I am quite content to let the facts speak for themselves.
State the facts.
I am quite convinced that my hon. friend never mentioned the Vancouver hotel during his election campaign. That is what he says and I accept his word.
I said more than that.
More than that?
Yes.
Nobody on my hon. friend's behalf mentioned the Vancouver hotel.

There was no such appeal made on my behalf.

I accept that statement- that neither my hon. friend nor anybody on his behalf in his election campaign-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Nor any newspaper.
Nor any newspaper, nor anyone with whom my hon. friend had to do for the purpose of getting elected mentioned the Vancouver hotel.
Oh, oh.

But referring to matters specifically before the House, the hon. member for West Calgary referred to my statement that in regard to every item here mentioned as being "on order" the railway company had sufficient money to pay for that equipment when delivered.
That was not the question at all.

My hon. friend read out a few items of the long list I read this afternoon and which had following them the statement "on order". I have totalled up the amount involved and if my figures are correct, and I believe they are, it amounts to $833,000 out of a proposed expenditure of twenty million. I would point out to the House that one-third of the total thirty-one millions which is now before the House was voted at the last session of parliament, that the money was paid out to the Canadian National Railways, and I make the statement that .it was quite proper for the Canadian National Railway Company to pay for that portion of the equipment which is "on order" -that they were quite right in doing so. As to the orders in council to which my hon. friend refers, outlining the purposes for which the advances were made to the Canadian National Railway Company while he was Minister of Finance, I have not received them, but I have sent for them.
They were made before my time.
I understand there were orders in council.
That is what I say. There were seven and a half millions obtained before our time.
And two and a half millions since.
After you came back.
Yes. The point is, in connection with the small proportion of this proposal which is "on order", that there is authority to pay the money required to be paid.
That money has been all spent otherwise.
No.
The whole of the ten millions has been spent otherwise. The deputy will tell you that. I know whereof I speak.

May I say that I live in
British Columbia and have access to the daily papers published in Vancouver. As a loyal British Columbian I feel somewhat inclined to support the attitude of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who made a reasonable statement as to the claims of that city. I certainly hope they get the hotel built if they are entitled to it. But when it comes to statements made by his colleagues that they never in any way used this question to promote their political ambitions I must take them with a great deal of gravity. I heard the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) this evening describe what he considered was the nature of that transaction. He called it a contract but he admitted in answer to a question from the Minister of Railways that it was a contract that was not signed by the railway company. That would be somewhat similar to the position of a man who might come to me and say "I have sold you a house". To that I would say, "Oh, have you, I did not know it." "Oh, yes, I have sold you a house because I have got the contract signed." To that I would say, "Have you? I did not sign it," evoking a reply, "No, but I signed it." That is the position the hon. member for West Calgary tells us was the correct one. But that was not the position that was represented to the people of Vancouver. I did not hear those hon. gentlemen say anything about the matter, but in the newspapers friendly to them there was displayed, in such big headlines that there was barely room for anything else on the page, "The contract is signed". There was nothing mentioned to show that it was signed only by the contractor ar.d not by the railway company; that point was not brought out. That modification was not set forth even in the small print that is customary in setting forth the composition of patent medicines. That important detail was omitted entirely. Of oourse I was more particularly interested in the election in Comox-Albemi, but I saw the daily papers of Vancouver and I would say offhand and subject to criticism that as near as I could guess the campaign of their party in that city consisted to .the extent of one-

third, customs scandal, one-third attacking the old age pension legislation, and one-third enthusing about the building of this big hotel.
Did the minister make the statement that the value of these orders amounted to only $800,000?

I calculated the amount from the sheet supplied me by the management and which I lent a few moments ago to my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett)-that is I calculated the items stated to be "on order". It is true that within the last few days, knowing the near approach of the session of parliament, orders may have been given with the assurance that parliament was going to deal with the matter, subject to cancellation before any work was done. Even from a technical standpoint I cannot see that the management has not been correct in giving orders subject to the authority of parliiment.

The minister made the statement that it was the intention of the Canadian National Railway management to spend in the United States a portion of the money to be used in purchasing equipment for the American lines forming part of the system. I should like to point out to him the situation in southern Ontario. Despite the tremendous traffic that part of Canada yields American lines, they have in the last few years practically reduced the eonst-uction of car? and the repairs done in their shops in Ontario to a minimum. The result has been that many men have been laid off and the local municipalities have a serious situation to deal with. Is there any way by which this House can compel the American lines operating in that part of Canada to give to Canadian workmen a portion of the work that justly belongs to them? Last year in the estimates there was an appropriation to build new shops for the Canadian National at St. Thomas. I ask the Minister of Railways if it is still the intention of the railway management to go on with these shops, and if not what reason they assign for changing their plans.
I found it rather difficult to hear my hon. friend but I gather that his remarks had relation to the desirability of getting as much of this work done in Canada as possible. Am I correct in that?

I should like to point out that in the last few years the American lines have practically discontinued the construction of new cars and are doing no major repairing. They have shops equipped for

that purpose but they a.re not using them; they are not making any major repairs in Canada. I am speaking about the Michigan Central Railway in particular. Are there any customs regulations or anything that would compel them to do a proportionate share of this work in Canada?

As I stated this afternoon, the Customs department is watching the situation in that regard; but I would point out to my hon. friend that a great deal of American equipment passes from the United States into Canada and out again just in the same manner as our equipment does, and in such cases the customs regulations of both countries permit the passage through and repairs can be made on either side. I shall be glad to make further inquiries in reference to the point raised by my hon. friend which really has no bearing upon the particular estimates before the committee, although this is a proper time to mention it in any event.

I know the minister
will be very glad to have his attention directed to the fact that the national railway makes contractual commitments before parliament has voted the money, because in the Kingston Standard-Whig of Wednesday I find a despatch from Montreal indicating that the first of a series of orders was received on Saturday by the Canadian Car and Foundry Company, Limited, for $2,000,000 for some of the very equipment that has been mentioned to-day and that orders are now to go to Kingston, to tihe locomotive company for the work that has to be done there. Apparently this is an inspired despatch because it describes where the contracts are to go with regard to the Grand Trunk eastern lines. I merely state that this illustrates the point I was endeavouring to make, namely that the railway company makes contractual commitments before parliament has voted the money, and it is desirable that there should be some uniform system with respect to the matter if it is to be followed along the line suggested by the minister himself. This record indicates clearly what is taking place with respect to the Canadian Car and Foundry Company.

My (hon. friend will
surely recognize that that article says merely what the newspaper believes has happened.

It is a despatch from
Montreal.

Quite likely, but it is
not a Canadian National official statement.

Yes it is. It says that
they have placed orders for new equipment.
Who says that?
The newspaper says that the Canadian National has done so.

It does not officially
quote the Canadian National.

We will ascertain if the
contracts have not been made.

My information regarding that point is simply this:	The railway
company has been pressing very hard to be allowed to get into a position where this equipment will be on order, as much of it will be very badly required before it is delivered and deliveries will stretch over a year or 'more of this particular equipment. Sir Henry Thornton on the last occasion when he discussed the matter with me stated, "I must move forward." I said, "Very well, there is nothing to prevent you from going through all the preliminaries of calling for tenders and getting your prices so that you will be in a position to act with the utmost expedition once we have dealt with the matter in parliament."
Will the minister inquire whether or not on Saturday last a contract was let to the Canadian Car and Foundry Company for $2,000,000 worth of equipment, and let parliament know the result?
I will.
If he does I am satisfied he will find that a contract has been let.

The deputy minister is
a director of the company and he advises me definitely that such a contract has not been let.

subtopic: SUPPLY BILL

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the House go into committee of ways and means.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

subtopic: SUPPLY BILL
speechtext: Resolved that towards making good the supply granted to His Majesty on account of certain expenses of the public service for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1927, the sum of $21,400,000 be granted out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.

Motion agreed to.
Resolution, reported and concurred an. Mr. Dunning thereupon moved for leave 'to introduce Bill No. 58, for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending March 31, 1927.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.
